newsitem.title: NORWAY: Asian oil product tankers prospects seen strong.
newsitem.headline: Asian oil product tankers prospects seen strong.

text.p: Oil product tankers should profit further from the booming Asian oil market, shipping brokers said on Wednesday.

"The most significant emerging trade is that between Japan and South Korea," said Colin Cridland, newly appointed director of tanker project analysis at London shipbroker Simpson, Spence and Young Ltd.
"There is a much stronger market growing for product carriers, particularly in the 35,000 deadweight (dwt) to 40,000 dwt range," he told the Nor-Shipping '97 conference here.

"The product carrier segment looks promising for some years ahead, particularly as the orderbook is not excessive," said Jarle Hammer, director of research at Fearnsearch, a unit of Norway's Fearnleys AS.

Cridland described the Asia-Pacific region as also having great potential for longhaul tanker trades, although he stressed that rising consumption would be most likely to benefit very large crude carrier (VLCC) operators.

He said oil consumption in the region had risen by 71 percent over the last decade and that net import requirements were estimated to grow from 9.4 million barrels per day (bpd) in 1997 to 11.7 million bpd in 2000 and 14.9 million bpd by the year 2005.
Cridland said that translated into an extra 13 milion tones a year to the year 2000, which would require an extra 16 VLCCs loading in the Mideast Gulf a year.
However, rising Asian demand for sweeter crude from West Africa, from 13 percent of its imports to around 25 percent in the next three years, could equate to an extra 54 vessels being required.

But he balanced optimism with the warning that 40 VLCCs were currently on order and scrapping of 25 year old tankers should not necessarily be expected. They could now possibly live on to 30 years of age with hydrostatically balanced loading, he cautioned.
